title: Whatever you ask
hook: whatever you ask of your own Master, He gives (Dhanasri M5, ang 681)
tomorrow: As the Word comes to me, Lalo

segments.voice: Yesterday, one father, and your line: all his children. Which stranger did you treat like a sibling? Today, the week closes with a bold promise about asking. Day six hundred fifty-eight.

Every kid learns, early, which parent to ask. Dad for the late curfew, Mom for the money, Grandma for the extra dessert. Asking is a skill. You learn who will say yes, and how to phrase it, and when to wait. Then one day, in Raag Dhanasri, you come across a line from Guru Arjan that seems to skip all of that strategy: whatever you ask of your own Master, He gives. No angles. No timing. It sounds almost too simple. So what is it actually saying?
screen: `WHICH PARENT TO ASK.` → `ASKING IS A SKILL.` → `WHATEVER YOU ASK, HE GIVES.`

segments.voice: The line is on ang 681: jo maageh thaakur apune te, soee soee devai. Whatever is asked of one's own Master, that very thing He gives. And it continues, in effect: whatever the servant Nanak speaks, it comes true, here and hereafter. Thaakur is master, lord, the one you belong to. Notice the small word apune, your own. Not a distant ruler you petition through officials. Your own Master, the one who already knows you. Now, the honest question. Does this mean a person gets anything they want? Sikh teachers generally read it in context. The one asking in this hymn is the daas, the servant, someone who has lived close to the Master long enough that their wants have started to take His shape. Gurbani also speaks constantly of bhaana, the Will, and of asking first for the Name. So the line is less a blank check than a picture of trust between a servant and a good master: the servant isn't afraid to ask, and the Master doesn't hold back. Sikhs also say, from experience, that what's given is sometimes not what was asked, but what was needed: strength instead of escape, patience instead of speed. Look back at the week. Partners, all: everyone holds a share. You are my father. Make mercy your mosque. You spent the night sleeping: not for a shell. A child is born, a gift arrives. One father, all his children. And now: whatever you ask. A week about belonging, and about asking like someone who belongs.
screen: `THAAKUR: YOUR OWN MASTER.` · `THE SERVANT WHO ASKS IN TRUST.` · `NOT A BLANK CHECK: THE WILL.` · `THIS WEEK: BELONGING, THEN ASKING.` · then, large: `ASK YOUR MASTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for one good thing. Sit quietly and let your wants come up, all of them, the big and the petty. Don't judge them. Then let them settle, and see which one is truly good: good for you and good for others. Maybe it's courage, or healing for someone, or patience with a child. Choose that one. If you pray, you can ask the One for it simply, the way a child asks a parent they trust. If you don't, hold it as a hope. The bell holds the time.
Whatever you ask. Guru Arjan: whatever is asked of one's own Master, He gives; the trust of a servant who belongs.
Your line: ask your master. Today, ask plainly for one good thing, from the One if you pray, or from a person you trust. Then notice what's given. Day six hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Arjan's Dhanasri shabad in kirtan and often recall its line 'jo maageh thaakur apune te soee soee devai' when making an Ardas, alongside acceptance of the Will.

fork.setup: you've read: whatever you ask of your own Master, He gives. what do you ask for?
options: one truly good thing, in trust.
nothing; it's too good to be true.
fork.reveal: the line describes a servant close enough to the Master that the asking takes the Master's shape.

original.note: Gurmukhi: master, lord; jo maageh thaakur apune te, whatever is asked of one's own Master.

trapdoor: what you thought: pray and you'll get what you want.
what it means: a servant who belongs can ask without fear, and the Master gives.
what a scholar hears: the promise is framed by the daas relationship and by Gurbani's wider teaching on bhaana and asking for naam; read alone, it is often misheard as transactional.
